title: CBA ramps up pressure on regulator over Macquarie capital settings
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank is ratcheting up the pressure on financial regulators to rein in Macquarie’s use of a corporate structure it alleges provides an unfair competitive advantage, after commissioning economic analysis to show how the arrangement supports Macquarie’s rapid growth in mortgages and deposits.
The analysis by Mandala, obtained by The Australian Financial Review, questions whether the settings applied to Macquarie by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority create an uneven playing field by allowing it to operate with a lower capital base than major banks.
The structure – known as a “non-operating holding company” – allows an APRA-regulated bank to put businesses that do not involve holding deposits into a non-bank entity with lighter regulation.
Macquarie created its non-operating holding company in 2007; the non-bank contains its asset management and investment banking divisions, along with some of its commodities operations. The idea behind separating banking and non-bank businesses is to give the latter more flexibility to compete with players that are not prudentially regulated, such as private equity firms.
However, Mandala argues the structure has allowed Macquarie’s banking operations to report a common equity tier 1 capital ratio – a key measure of a bank’s financial security – that understates its true risk exposure. That’s because some of its risky investment, trading and asset management activity occurs in the non-bank group, which is excluded from CET1 capital calculations.
APRA said in its 2026-27 corporate plan published on August 20 that it would review existing authorisations for banks with non-operating holding companies and report back in the first half of next calendar year.
Macquarie rejects any suggestion of unequal treatment, saying its bank is subject to the same prudential standards as the major banks. It says its structure reflects its global, non-retail banking operations, which domestic banks don’t have and which continue to drive most of Macquarie’s earnings.
The commissioning of the expert economic analysis – which CBA plans to use in discussions with APRA – comes seven months after Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn publicly aired concerns about the structure.
At CBA’s interim results in February, Comyn pointed to an unnamed competitor “optimising around capital, regulatory structure, regulatory architecture.” It was obviously a reference to Macquarie, which has been outpacing the growth of CBA and all other banks in home loans and deposits for several years.
Three weeks later, at The Australian Financial Review Business Summit, Macquarie chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake told Comyn that Macquarie plays “in the jurisdictions that we are in by the rules they have”, adding that Australia’s banking regulations are the strongest of any country that Macquarie operates in.
The high-stakes quarrel between the mortgage market juggernauts went up a gear the following week when CBA chairman Paul O’Malley raised concerns about “uneven regulatory treatment” in a speech to company directors.
The issue will be known to new Macquarie chief executive Greg Ward, who ran the banking and financial services division before being elevated to replace Wikramanayake in November.
Mandala said the arrangements raised a policy question about whether the settings “remain fit for purpose in the current banking landscape ... whether they align risk, capital, supervision, loss-absorbing capacity and public confidence, given material changes in prudential standards, market scale, funding models and group complexity over the past two decades.”
But any “reform should be grounded in system design rather than competitive grievance,” the report added.
The consultants found that Macquarie’s reduced capital cost base has allowed it to offer better interest rates for savings to increase deposit market share. The report argues major bank capital requirements have quadrupled since 2007, while rules for Macquarie had remained unchanged.
Macquarie says the prudential capital requirements applicable to its bank have changed over time, in line with reforms to the prudential framework and consistent with changes for major banks. It points out the level 2 CET1 capital ratio reported by its bank is consistently higher than major bank average ratios.
“The report seems to confuse estimated measurements for the entire Macquarie Group with the actual measurements applied for Macquarie Bank’s standalone operations, and fails to acknowledge the fact that Macquarie Bank’s activities cannot be subsidised by the group’s predominantly international non-bank activities,” a Macquarie spokeswoman said.
“There is a level playing field with regards to the capital that Macquarie Bank is allocated and measured against with respect to major banks.”
APRA said the outcomes of individual reviews of the structure, which is used by a handful of other banks, would not be published, but any updates to non-operating holding company authorisations would be made public.
APRA began work in 2022 on developing a new prudential standard for non-operating holding companies but stopped after the 2023 banking turmoil in Europe and the United States that saw Credit Suisse and Silicon Valley Bank collapse, causing ructions across global markets and forcing the regulator to reassess its treatment of hybrid debt instruments.
The prudential regulator has decided not to resume work on a new prudential standard, but instead undertake the review of its legacy banking non-operating holding company authorisations, the spokesman said.
“As with any review, APRA will consider a range of information and views, noting the review is not being undertaken in response to any single entity or issue.”
Macquarie continues to grow at a much faster rate than CBA and all other banks according to statistics released by APRA two weeks ago. It now has a 7 per cent share of the mortgage market, up by a full percentage point over the past 12 months.
Macquarie followed CBA in cutting home loan interest rates in July, as the two battle it out in a mortgage price war.
In March, O’Malley told an Australian Institute of Company Directors event that bank capital rules play a crucial role in ensuring Australia’s lenders have strong balance sheets and can support the economy by lending during periods of financial volatility.
But “across multiple sectors, we are seeing uneven regulatory treatment for functionally similar services,” he said.
ANZ also created a non-operating holding company in January 2023. It is subject to stricter conditions than Macquarie’s, including that all lending needs to reside within the bank. AMP, Judo, MyState and Revolut also operate APRA-regulated non-operating holding companies.
Macquarie has continued to tweak where various businesses sit within its group. For example, it shifted part of its commodities trading unit out of its banking entity last September, citing the growth of its energy business in North America that provides risk management, physical execution and logistics services which it said were better suited outside a bank.
